title: Small molecule inhibitors of eIF4A1/2 impair the oxidative stress response in osteosarcoma cells to block tumor growth and metastatic capacity
projectDescription: Effective therapies for metastatic osteosarcoma (OS) remain a major clinical unmet need. Targeting mRNA translation in metastatic OS represents an attractive option, as selective translation under stress supports the rapid synthesis of cytoprotective proteins that facilitate metastatic competence. We therefore assessed eukaryotic translation factors in OS, revealing high expression of eIF4A1 in metastatic OS. The eIF4A1 inhibitor, CR-1-31B, potently inhibited metastatic OS growth in vitro and reduced lung tumor burden in orthotopic mouse models. CR-1-31B synergized with the oxidative stress inducer, tert-butylhydroquinone (tBHQ), to enhance cell death under oxidative stress. Proteomic analysis revealed a subset of proteins that were upregulated by tBHQ alone, but inhibited by co-treatment of CR-1-31B, most notably the NRF2 antioxidant transcription factor, and NRF2 inactivation phenocopied CR-1-31B in blocking OS lung metastasis in vivo. Collectively, our data reveal that targeting eIF4A1 with CR-1-31B is highly effective in blocking OS metastasis by blunting the NRF2 antioxidant response.
sampleProcessingProtocol: The total proteome material separated as part of the polysome isolation was first digested with a mixture of 1 Unit of benzonase nuclease and 1µg of RNaseA for 10-minutes at 21°C. After, cell disruption was completed through addition of a 4X lysis buffer (400mM HEPES pH 7.3, 8% (v/v) SDS, 40mM dithiothreitol) to a final 1X concentration, and mixtures incubated at 95°C for 5-minutes. After heating, samples were left at 21°C for 10-minutes prior to the addition of chloroacetamide to a final concentration of 40mM and a further incubation at 21°C for 30-minutes. Excess chloroacetamide was quenched through the addition of additional dithiothreitol to a final concentration of 40mM. At this stage, protein samples were processed for DIA-MS. For DIA-MS analysis, protein lysates were initially processed using a modified version of the SP3 protocol. Specifically, 250µg of a combined and rinsed stock of Sera-Mag carboxylate-modified magnetic beads was combined with ~20µg protein lysate in a working volume of 100µL. Aggregation of proteins to the surface of the magnetic beads was driven via addition of acetone to a final proportion of 80% (v/v). SP3 reactions were incubated for 5-minutes at room temperature prior to centrifugation for 5-minutes at 5,000g. The supernatant was discarded, without the use of a magnetic rack, and the beads reconstituted in 800µL of 80% (v/v) ethanol prior to centrifugation at 5,000g for an additional 5-minutes. After supernatant removal, the magnetic beads were reconstituted in 100µL of 4M urea in 100mM HEPES pH 7.3 with trypsin + rLysC (1:10µg, enzyme:sample). Mixtures were incubated in a ThermoMixer at 30°C for 2-hours with shaking at 1,000rpm. Digestion mixtures were then diluted 1 in 4 with 100mM HEPES pH 7.3 to bring the final urea concentration to 1M, and incubated for an additional 16-hours at 30°C with shaking at 1,000rpm. Peptide-containing supernatants were recovered via centrifugation at 12,000g for 2-minutes along with utilization of a magnetic rack. Recovered peptides were desalted using Strata-X Polymeric SPE microelution plates by activating the column with methanol, rinsing with 0.1% (v/v) trifluoroacetic acid, sample binding, rinsing with 4% (v/v) methanol in 0.1% (v/v) formic acid, and final elution in 60% (v/v) methanol in 0.1% (v/v) formic acid. Desalted peptides were concentrated in a SpeedVac centrifuge and reconstituted in 1% DMSO in 1% formic acid.
dataProcessingProtocol: DIA-MS analysis was carried out on the Orbitrap Eclipse using the same LC configuration and settings as for DDA-MS analysis apart from a modified flow rate of 400nL/min. DIA-MS analysis was carried out on an Orbitrap Eclipse instrument equipped with an EASY-nLC 1200 liquid chromatography (LC) system. For analysis, peptide fractions were initially trapped on a pre-column (150µm x 3cm, 1.9µm C18 Reprosil-Pur Basic beads from Dr. Maisch) and then separated by an analytical column (150µm x 35cm, 1.9µm C18 Reprosil-Pur Basic beads, connected to a 20µm internal diameter LOTUS electrospray emitter from Fossil Ion Tech) with a 150-minute gradient at a flow rate of 200nL/min. Each sample was injected two individual times, with each injection covering analysis of a separate mass range (injection 1 = 398-644, 2 = 642 - 888). Specifically, the Orbitrap MS was globally set to use a positive ion spray voltage of 2000V, an ion transfer tube temperature of 275°C, a default charge state of 3, and an RF Lens setting of 60%. The complete duty cycle of the acquisition method consisted of two MS1 scans and two sets of windowed MS2 scans (order MS1 - MS2 - MS1 - MS2). For the first, low mass range injection, the initial MS1 scan covered a mass range of 396-646m/z at a resolution of 15,000 with an AGC target of 250% and a max injection time set to ‘Auto’. The following set of DIA MS2 scans covered a precursor range of 398-642m/z with an isolation window size of 4m/z (0m/z overlap) for a total of 61 scan events. Each scan used an stepped HCD energy (26%, 30%, 34%) and covered a defined mass range of 200-1800m/z at a resolution of 30,000 with a normalized AGC target of 2000%, and the maximum injection time set to ‘Auto’. Loop control was set to ‘Time’ with a value of 3-seconds. The next MS1 scan and following DIA MS2 used the same settings as the previous with the exception that the MS2 precursor mass range was set to 400-644m/z to give a 2m/z overlap with the previous scan windows. For the second, high mass range injection, the scan settings were as for the low mass injection with the following changes: 1. MS1 scan range of 640-890m/z; 2. DIA-MS2 precursor scan ranges of 642-886m/z and 644-888m/z. All scan data was acquired in centroid mode. DIA-MS raw data were de-multiplexed using msConvert, a command line utility program (ProteoWizard, peakPicking = ‘vendor’, demultiplex = overlap only, 10ppm, SIM as spectra) and processed using DIA-NN (version 1.8.1) (45). Specifically, a representative human proteome fasta database was provided to DIA-NN for library-free search (Trypsin/P, 1 missed cleavage, N-term M excision, C carbamidometylation, 2-4 precursor charge, 390-900 precursor m/z range) using a mass accuracy setting of 20ppm, a MS1 accuracy of 20ppm, a scan window of 0, unrelated runs, use isotopologues, MBR, no shared spectra, and a precursor FDR of 1% (protein inference = genes, neural network classifier = single-pass mode, quantification strategy = robust LC (high precision), cross-run normalization = RT-dependent, library generation = smart profiling). Resulting data were analyzed in R using the ‘iq’ package to generate estimates of protein abundance, and ‘DEqMS’ to perform differential abundance calculations between conditions.
